summary: Provides a general encoding for constraints imposed by network elements in GMPLS-controlled networks, such as asymmetric switching, label range limits and non-local label assignment, so these can be advertised for path computation.

plainLanguage.summary: In an optical network, a light signal that arrives on one fibre has to leave on a fibre that carries the same colour of light, and it has to follow a route the equipment can actually make. Each piece of equipment has its own limits on which input it can connect to which output and which wavelengths it can handle. This RFC defines a common way of writing those limits down, so that the routing system and the path computation element can exchange them instead of each working from its own assumptions.

questions: what is a gmpls connectivity matrix
what is a port label restriction
what is a label set in gmpls
subtitle: A shared binary format for saying which ports connect and which labels may be used, so optical and other GMPLS networks can plan paths.

tldr.problem: Some network elements cannot carry any signal from any input to any output. A wavelength-switched router cannot change the colour of a light signal, so a path may have to keep the same wavelength across the whole network, and each node has its own idea of which wavelengths it can reach. A path computation element that does not know these limits will propose paths that cannot be set up.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four encodings: a connectivity matrix that says which input ports and labels can reach which output ports, port label restrictions that say which labels a port may use, and two fields that advertise the labels currently available and those reserved for shared backup. The label and link sets use the action and range conventions of GMPLS signalling, extended with a bitmap form.
tldr.outcome: The information can be carried in OSPF, IS-IS or the PCE communication protocol, and the protocol-specific documents define how. The document itself asks for no number allocations, because the encodings are independent of any one protocol.

today: RFC 7579 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It asks for no allocations of its own: the protocol-specific documents that carry these encodings make those requests.

sections.title: Why Constraints Have to Be Advertised
sections.content:
Some data-plane technologies that wish to make use of a GMPLS control plane contain additional constraints on switching capability and label assignment. In addition, some of these technologies must perform non-local label assignment based on the nature of the technology, the wavelength continuity constraint in Wavelength Switched Optical Networks being an example. Such constraints can lead to the requirement for link-by-link label availability in path computation and label assignment.

The RFC provides efficient encodings of the information needed by the routing and label assignment process in technologies such as WSON, and they are potentially applicable to a wider range of technologies. The encodings can be used to extend GMPLS signalling and routing protocols, and they could also be used by other mechanisms to convey the same information to a path computation element.

The encodings are for the information elements defined in RFC 7446 that have applicability to WSON. They are designed to be suitable for use in the GMPLS routing protocols OSPF (RFC 4203) and IS-IS (RFC 5307), and in the PCE Communication Protocol (RFC 5440). The information distributed in OSPF and IS-IS is arranged by the nesting of sub-TLVs within TLVs, and this document defines elements to be used within such constructs; the specific constructs of sub-TLVs and their nesting are left to the protocol enhancement documents.
sections.plainLanguage:
Ordinary packet routing has a simple model: a router can usually take a packet arriving on any port and send it out of any other. Optical networks are not like that. A wavelength-switched router cannot turn red light into blue light, so a signal has to keep its colour from end to end, and a path across several routers has to be arranged so the colour works at every one of them.

Each router also has its own idea of which wavelengths it can reach, so the path has to be worked out link by link. The information needed for that has to travel with the routes, and this RFC defines how it is written down, in a way that is independent of the routing protocol.

sections.title: Constraints on Which Ports Connect
sections.content:
For some network elements, the ability of a signal or packet on a particular input port to reach a particular output port may be limited. In some network elements, such as a simple multiplexer, the connectivity between some input and output ports may be fixed. To take such constraints into account during path computation, this aspect of a network element is modelled with a connectivity matrix.

The connectivity matrix represents either the potential connectivity matrix for asymmetric switches or the fixed connectivity for an asymmetric device such as a multiplexer. The matrix does not represent any particular internal blocking behaviour, but indicates which input ports and labels, for example wavelengths, could possibly be connected to a particular output port and label pair. Representing internal state-dependent blocking for a node is beyond the scope of the document, and because of its highly implementation-dependent nature it would most likely not be subject to standardization in the future.

The matrix is a conceptual M by N matrix, where M is the number of input ports, each with m labels, and N the number of output ports, each with n labels.
sections.plainLanguage:
The first kind of constraint is about reachability inside one device. Which input ports can feed which output ports? For a switch, that depends on how it is configured, so the matrix describes what could be connected in principle. For a device such as a multiplexer, where the connections are fixed in the hardware, the matrix simply records the fixed wiring.

What the matrix does not do is describe the state of the device at a particular moment. Whether a given input can reach a given output right now may also depend on which other paths are in use, and that is a property of each implementation rather than something that can be standardised.

sections.title: Constraints on Which Labels May Be Used
sections.content:
If the nature of the equipment involved in a network results in a requirement for non-local label assignment, the constraints can be based on limits imposed by the ports themselves and on those implied by the current label usage. Such constraints only become important when label assignment has a non-local character. In MPLS, for example, a router may have a limited range of labels available for use on an output port and a set of labels already in use on that port, which are therefore unavailable for use. This information does not need to be shared unless there is some limitation on the router's label swapping ability. If a Time Division Multiplexer node lacks the ability to perform time-slot interchange, or a WSON node lacks the ability to perform wavelength conversion, then the label assignment process is not local to a single node, and it may be advantageous to share the label assignment constraint information for use in path computation.

Port label restrictions model the label restrictions that the network element and link may impose on a port. They say what labels may or may not be used on a link, and they are intended to be relatively static. More dynamic information is contained in the information on available labels. Port label restrictions are specified relative to the port in general or to a specific connectivity matrix, for increased modelling flexibility.
sections.plainLanguage:
The second kind of constraint is about labels, which in an optical network are wavelengths. A port may only carry certain wavelengths, and only a limited number of them at once. Some of this is fixed: the port simply cannot carry a wavelength it was never built to carry. Some of it is about what is already running on the port, which changes as paths are set up and torn down.

The fixed part is worth advertising on its own, because it explains why a path is impossible. A node that cannot convert wavelengths has to keep the same wavelength across the whole path, so the label assigned at one end constrains the whole route. That is why the label has to be chosen for the entire path rather than hop by hop.

sections.title: The Connectivity Matrix Field
sections.content:
The Connectivity Matrix Field represents how input ports are connected to output ports for network elements. The switch and fixed connectivity matrices can be compactly represented in terms of a minimal list of input and output port set pairs that have mutual connectivity, and such a minimal list representation leads naturally to a graph representation for path computation purposes, involving the fewest additional nodes and links.

The field is uniquely identified only by the advertising node, and there may be more than one Connectivity Matrix Field associated with a node, because a node can partition the switch matrix into several sub-matrices. The partitioning is primarily to limit the size of any individual information element used to represent the matrix and to enable incremental updates. When the matrix is partitioned into sub-matrices, each sub-matrix is mutually exclusive of the others in representing which ports and labels are associated with it, so two matrices will not have the same combination of source port, source label, destination port and destination label. Each sub-matrix is identified by a different Matrix ID, which MUST represent a unique combination of those four values.

The encoding holds a Connectivity field of 4 bits giving the device type, where 0 means the device is fixed and 1 means it is switched, for example a Reconfigurable Optical Add/Drop Multiplexer or Optical Cross-Connect. The MatrixID is an 8-bit integer, and the value 0xFF is reserved for use with port label restrictions and should not be used to identify a connectivity matrix. The rest of the field is reserved, and then come Link Set A and Link Set B, which together represent a pair of link sets. There are two permitted combinations for the direction parameter of link sets A and B.

In the first, Link Set A is an input and Link Set B an output, and the meaning of the pair is that any signal that inputs a link in set A can potentially be switched out of an output link in set B. In the second, both are bidirectional, and the meaning is that any signal that inputs on the links in set A can potentially output on a link in set B, and any input signal on the links in set B can potentially output on a link in set A. If link set A is an input and link set B an output for a signal, then it implies that link set A is an output and link set B an input for that signal.
sections.plainLanguage:
The matrix is not written out as a grid. It is written as a list of pairs of port groups, where each pair says that anything arriving on one group of ports can be sent out of the other group. That is a much shorter way of saying the same thing, and it converts neatly into the graph that the path computation works on.

A node may advertise more than one matrix, each with its own number, so that the information can be split into pieces that are small enough to send and can be updated one at a time. The pieces do not overlap: no port and label combination appears in two of them.

sections.title: Port Label Restrictions
sections.content:
The Port Label Restrictions Field says what labels may or may not be used on a link. More than one of these fields may be needed to fully specify a complex port constraint, and when more than one is present the resulting restriction is the union of the restrictions expressed in each field. The use of the reserved value 0xFF for the MatrixID indicates that a restriction applies to the port and not to a specific connectivity matrix.

The field holds a MatrixID, which is either the value in the corresponding Connectivity Matrix Field or takes the value 0xFF to indicate that the restriction applies to the port regardless of any connectivity matrix. The RstType, or restriction type, can take five values. A value of 0 is SIMPLE_LABEL, a simple label selective restriction, where the accompanying label set indicates the labels permitted on the port or matrix. A value of 1 is CHANNEL_COUNT, where the accompanying maximum number of channels indicates the maximum number of channels, that is labels, that can be simultaneously used on the port or matrix; that number is a 32-bit integer. A value of 2 is LABEL_RANGE, for a label range device with a movable centre label and width, which is a generalization of the waveband device; the maximum label range, a 32-bit integer, indicates the maximum width of the waveband in terms of the channel spacing given in the label set, and the corresponding label set indicates the overall tuning range. A value of 3 combines SIMPLE_LABEL and CHANNEL_COUNT, where the label set and the maximum number of channels indicate the labels permitted on the port and the maximum number that can be used at once. A value of 4 is LINK_LABEL_EXCLUSIVITY, where the accompanying link set indicates that a label may be used at most once among the ports in that set.

The switching capability is defined in RFC 4203 and the LSP encoding type in RFC 3471. Together these fields define the type of labels used in specifying the restrictions and the interface type to which they apply. A final optional field carries additional restriction parameters for each restriction type that pertain to specific protocols.
sections.plainLanguage:
This field carries the limits on a port: which wavelengths it may carry, how many at once, and whether a wavelength may be used on more than one of a set of ports.

There are five kinds of restriction, and a port can carry more than one of them, in which case the limits are the union of what each one says. The MatrixID says which ports the restriction applies to: either a particular entry in the connectivity matrix, or the whole port.

sections.title: Link Sets and Label Sets
sections.content:
Properties of groups of links are often needed, and to describe them efficiently a link set concept is used, similar to the label set concept of RFC 3471. The Link Set Field is used in the connectivity matrix. Its Action field of 8 bits has two values: an inclusive list, which indicates that one or more link identifiers are included in the set, each identifying a separate link that is part of it; and an inclusive range, which indicates that the set defines a range of links, containing two link identifiers, the first indicating the start of the range and the second the end, with all links with numeric values between the bounds considered part of the set. A value of zero in either position indicates that there is no bound on the corresponding portion of the range, and the inclusive range action can be set only when the identifier for unnumbered link is used.

The Dir field gives the directionality of the link set in 2 bits: 0 for bidirectional, 1 for input and 2 for output. In optical networks one thinks in terms of unidirectional and bidirectional links, and label restrictions or connectivity may differ for an input port than for its companion output port, if one exists. Interfaces such as those in the Interfaces MIB are assumed to be bidirectional, and so are the links advertised in the link state routing protocols.

The Format field gives the format of the link identifier in 6 bits: 0 for a link local identifier, which is supplied in the context of the advertising node; 1 for the local interface IPv4 address; and 2 for the local interface IPv6 address. All the link identifiers in the same list must be of the same type. The Length field is 16 bits and gives the total length of the Link Set Field in bytes. The link identifier represents the port being described, and can be the link local identifier of GMPLS routing; using that format can result in more compact encodings when the assignments are done reasonably.

The Label Set Field is used inside the Available Labels Field and the Shared Backup Labels Field, and inside the SIMPLE_LABEL, LABEL_RANGE and SIMPLE_LABEL with CHANNEL_COUNT restrictions. Its general format uses the Action concept of RFC 3471, with an additional action to define a bitmap type of label set. The Action field of 4 bits has five values: 0 for an inclusive list, 1 for an exclusive list, 2 for an inclusive range, 3 for an exclusive range and 4 for a bitmap set. Num Labels is a 12-bit integer, generally the number of labels, with a specific meaning depending on the action, and Length is the length in bytes of the whole Label Set Field.

For inclusive and exclusive lists, the first label is the one to be included or excluded and the last label is the last one, and Num Labels MUST match the number of labels. For inclusive and exclusive ranges, the start label is the first label in the range to be included or excluded and the end label is the last, and Num Labels MUST be two. For a bitmap set, Num Labels gives the number of labels the bitmap represents, each bit standing for one label with a value of 1 or 0 saying whether it is in the set, bit position zero being the lowest label and corresponding to the base label, and each succeeding position the next label above it. The bitmap is Num Labels bits long, padded out to a full multiple of 32 bits so that the field is a multiple of four bytes, and bits that do not represent labels SHOULD be set to zero and MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage:
Two building blocks are used throughout. A link set names a group of ports, either as a list or as a range of numbered ports, and it says whether the group is an input, an output or both. A label set names a group of wavelengths, and it comes in five forms: a list of the ones included, a list of the ones excluded, a range of ones included, a range of ones excluded, and a bitmap in which each bit stands for one wavelength.

All of them follow the conventions that GMPLS signalling already uses for label sets, so an implementation that already handles those will find these familiar. The bitmap form is the addition.

sections.title: Available Labels and Shared Backup Labels
sections.content:
The Available Labels Field consists of priority flags and a single variable-length Label Set Field. The priority flags are an 8-bit bitmap used to indicate which priorities are being advertised, in ascending order, with the leftmost bit representing priority level 0, the highest, and the rightmost bit representing priority level 7, the lowest. A bit MUST be set for each priority represented in the field and MUST NOT be set when the corresponding priority is not represented. If a label is available at priority M, it MUST be advertised as available at each priority N less than M, and at least one priority level MUST be advertised.

The priority field indicates the availability of the labels for use in LSP setup and preemption as described in RFC 3209. When a label is advertised as available for priorities 0 to M, it may be used by any LSP of priority N no greater than M. When a label is in use by an LSP of priority M, it may be used by an LSP of priority N less than M if LSP preemption is supported. When a label was initially advertised as available for priorities 0 to M, and is then used for an LSP at priority N with N no greater than M, the label is advertised as available for 0 to N-1.

The Shared Backup Labels Field has the same form: priority flags and a single variable-length Label Set Field, with the same rules about the bitmap and the same LSP setup and preemption rules.
sections.plainLanguage:
These two fields say which wavelengths are free to use, and separately which are held back for a backup path. Both carry a byte of priority flags: one bit for each of the eight priority levels, with level 0 the most important.

The rule about priorities is that a wavelength advertised for a given priority is also advertised for every higher priority. When a wavelength is taken by a path, it is then advertised only for the priorities above the one that took it, which is how a more important path can displace a less important one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document defines protocol-independent encodings for WSON information and introduces no security issues of its own. However, other documents that make use of these encodings within protocol extensions need to consider the issues and risks associated with inspection, interception, modification or spoofing of any of this information. It is expected that any such documents will describe the necessary security measures to provide adequate protection, and a general discussion of security in GMPLS networks can be found in RFC 5920.
sections.plainLanguage: The encodings themselves carry no security risk, because they only say how to write down information that the surrounding protocol already carries. The documents that put these fields into OSPF, IS-IS or the path computation protocol are the ones that have to think about whether the information can be read, changed or forged on the way.

viz.caption: THE HEADER OF THE CONNECTIVITY MATRIX FIELD

fields.name: Conn
fields.desc: The device type: 0 for a fixed device, 1 for a switched one.

fields.name: MatrixID
fields.desc: Identifies the matrix. The value 0xFF is reserved for port label restrictions.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved, followed by the pairs of link sets that carry the connectivity.

viz.caption: THE HEADER OF THE PORT LABEL RESTRICTIONS FIELD

fields.name: MatrixID
fields.desc: The matrix this restriction applies to, or 0xFF for the whole port.

fields.name: Switching Cap
fields.desc: The switching capability, as defined in RFC 4203.

fields.name: Encoding
fields.desc: The LSP encoding type, as defined in RFC 3471.

viz.caption: THE HEADER OF THE LABEL SET FIELD

fields.name: Action
fields.desc: The form of the set: 0 inclusive list, 1 exclusive list, 2 inclusive range, 3 exclusive range, 4 bitmap.

fields.name: Num Labels
fields.desc: The number of labels, with a meaning that depends on the action.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: The length in bytes of the whole Label Set Field.

viz.caption: THE KINDS OF PORT LABEL RESTRICTION

items.label: SIMPLE_LABEL
items.desc: The accompanying label set gives the labels permitted on the port.

items.label: CHANNEL_COUNT
items.desc: The accompanying maximum number of channels gives how many labels may be used at once.

items.label: LABEL_RANGE
items.desc: A device with a movable centre label and width; the maximum range gives the waveband width and the label set the tuning range.

items.label: SIMPLE_LABEL and CHANNEL_COUNT
items.desc: Both at once: the labels permitted on the port and how many may be used simultaneously.

items.label: LINK_LABEL_EXCLUSIVITY
items.desc: A label may be used at most once among the ports in the accompanying link set.

viz.caption: THE FIVE FORMS A LABEL SET CAN TAKE

items.title: Inclusive list
items.text: Action 0: the labels listed are the ones in the set.

items.title: Exclusive list
items.text: Action 1: the labels listed are the ones not in the set.

items.title: Inclusive range
items.text: Action 2: every label between the start and the end label is in the set.

items.title: Exclusive range
items.text: Action 3: every label between the start and the end label is not in the set.

items.title: Bitmap set
items.text: Action 4: one bit per label, from the lowest label upwards, saying whether it is in the set.
